hub_description: Investigate Kubernetes, Nginx and JSON logs with reproducible examples, real key sequences and explicit limits.
hub_note: All downloadable examples are synthetic. Guides describe Flik 0.3.0 and distinguish shell commands, in-app queries and investigation commands.
cta_text: Download a ready-to-run macOS or Linux release, open a synthetic sample and repeat the investigation locally.

guides.title: Filter Kubernetes JSON logs interactively
guides.description: Make container JSON readable, stack service and error filters, then undo one condition while your investigation stays open.
guides.scope: Flik 0.3.0 · synthetic examples · macOS and Linux
guides.body:
A pod log stream is easy to start and harder to investigate. Nested JSON hides the message, one service produces most of the noise, and every extra condition can mean rebuilding a shell pipeline. This guide keeps that work inside one Flik workspace.

Start with a saved example

Download the synthetic CRI sample. It contains timestamps, stdout/stderr streams and embedded application JSON. No cluster or production logs are needed.

flik container.log

Flik opens at the end. Press g to inspect the sample from its beginning, or G to return to the end. Press w to expand embedded JSON and inspect the service, severity and message without manually unescaping each record.

Stack two filters and undo one

  1. Press 3, enter service:payment, then press Enter.
  2. Press 3 again and enter level:error.
  3. Inspect the remaining payment errors. In the supplied five-record sample, the messages are upstream timeout and payment request failed.
  4. Press x. The error filter is removed while the payment-service filter remains. The warning about the connection pool becomes visible again.

This is a refinement workflow: undoing the last condition does not reopen the file or remove the preceding condition. Press Ctrl+F to inspect the filter stack.

Follow a live pod

kubectl logs -f deployment/demo-api | flik -

Replace deployment/demo-api with a workload you can read. Select the namespace or container using kubectl’s own flags when needed. Flik receives the application output; it does not connect to the Kubernetes API or choose a pod for you. Saved CRI files include the container wrapper; kubectl output may contain plain application JSON instead.

Watch the exact keys

The recording uses synthetic data and the actual Flik interface: beautify JSON, add a service filter, add an error filter, undo the last filter.

Know the boundary

Filters depend on fields that exist in the emitted format. Use Tab in search to complete available fields and observed values. If the data is plain text or uses different names, begin with a text search such as /timeout. Flik helps inspect the stream; it does not change Kubernetes retention, fetch events from other pods automatically or establish the cause of an incident.

guides.title: Find an error and the log lines before it
guides.description: Use smart find to keep the events surrounding an error, refine the result and return to the original file order.
guides.scope: Flik 0.3.0 · synthetic examples · macOS and Linux
guides.body:
An error line often describes the final symptom. The preceding line may show a failed connection, an exhausted pool or a retry. Filtering down to the word “error” can hide exactly the evidence you need. Flik’s smart find keeps matches together with a configurable amount of context.

Open the synthetic sample

Download the event sample, then open it locally. All names and identifiers are illustrative.

flik events.log

Press g to start at the beginning of a small file. A normal search such as /error narrows the view to matching lines. Smart find starts with a second slash.

Keep the preceding line

//error

Type the expression in the main log view and press Enter. Each matching line is shown with one preceding line. Context-only lines are visually distinguished from matches. They help explain the sequence, but they are not counted as additional occurrences.

Choose a larger window

//3,2:error

This keeps three lines before each match and two after. Overlapping windows are merged without duplicating lines, and the original file order is retained. Increase the window when a failure spans several operations; reduce it when surrounding traffic makes the result harder to read.

For a wider view around one selected result, press Ctrl+G. Inside that context view, n and p move between matches; Esc returns to the file.

Refine the incident

Add an include condition with 3 or an exclude condition with 8. Keep one change at a time so you can see what disappeared. Press x to undo the newest filter, or inspect the stack with Ctrl+F. A correlation ID can narrow the investigation further when unrelated requests share the same error text.

Watch context change the result

Use context as evidence

A line preceding an error is not automatically its cause. Concurrent requests can interleave, timestamps can be missing and services can buffer output. Check identifiers and time order before drawing a conclusion. Before sharing an incident export, review its redaction: recognized keys and patterns cannot guarantee removal of every application-specific secret.

guides.title: Count Nginx errors per hour
guides.description: Filter failed Nginx requests, count occurrences by hour and distinguish HTTP statuses from error-log severity.
guides.scope: Flik 0.3.0 · synthetic examples · macOS and Linux
guides.body:
A list of failed requests tells you what happened. A time histogram helps you see whether the same failure happened once, arrived in a burst or continued for hours. Flik applies its time report to the active filters, so the chart answers the question you just narrowed down.

Use a known access-log example

Download the five-request synthetic access log.

flik access.log

The sample contains three HTTP 200 responses, one 502 and one 503. All requests occur between 10:00 and 10:04 UTC on January 15, 2026. These are deliberately small, checkable inputs rather than a performance benchmark.

Filter server errors

  1. Press 3 to add an include rule.
  2. Enter status:5xx and confirm.
  3. Press H to count matching events by hour.

The expected hourly bucket is 2026-01-15 10:00 UTC: 2 matching requests. A 502 response and a 503 response each contribute one occurrence. The three successful requests do not contribute to this filtered histogram.

Change the time interval

Open the investigation prompt with Ctrl+K and enter:

histogram minute

The two error buckets are 10:02 and 10:03 UTC, with one request each. The same prompt accepts histogram hour and histogram day. Time reports are UTC snapshots; close and rerun the report to refresh it after the file changes.

Inspect an error log differently

An Nginx error log contains severity and diagnostic messages, not an HTTP response for every line. Download the error-log sample, open it with Flik and press S. When HTTP statuses are absent, the dashboard uses detected severity levels instead of an empty 2xx/3xx breakdown.

Check the scope before comparing

The S dashboard samples up to 5,000 lines. Frequency reports scan the full indexed source in the background, use recognized timestamps and exclude context-only lines from occurrence counts. Missing timestamps are reported separately. Custom log layouts may require raw-text inspection; do not treat an unrecognized status or timestamp as proof of no errors.

For a live issue, compare equal time windows and keep the same filter. A higher count can reflect more traffic rather than a higher failure rate; use a request denominator when you need a rate.

guides.title: Flik, grep and jq: choose the right log workflow
guides.description: Compare interactive log investigation with shell filtering and JSON transformation, using the same small example.
guides.scope: Flik 0.3.0 · synthetic examples · macOS and Linux
guides.body:
grep, jq and Flik are useful at different points in a log workflow. The practical choice depends on whether you want a repeatable pipeline or an investigation in which the next question changes after every result. This guide compares that workflow without claiming that Flik implements jq expressions.

Begin with the same JSON records

Download the five-record JSON Lines sample. It contains gateway, payment and worker messages. Two records have both service=payment and level=error.

Write a repeatable jq selection

jq -c 'select(.service == "payment" and .level == "error")' app.jsonl

This produces two matching JSON objects. It is a good fit for shell scripts, automated reports and pipelines where the transformation is known in advance. jq can also construct new objects and reshape JSON; those capabilities are outside Flik’s query language.

Investigate the same records in Flik

flik --table --fields timestamp,service,level,message app.jsonl

Press 3 and add service:payment, then add level:error. You see the same two error messages in an interactive view. Press x to remove only the latest filter: the payment warning becomes visible again without reopening the file. Use 6 to change columns and v to inspect distinct field values.

Choose by the task

TaskUseful starting point
Find a literal string in many text filesgrep or another text-search tool
Transform JSON and feed a scripted pipelinejq
Refine several log filters while retaining contextFlik
Follow a stream and change visible fields interactivelyFlik with stdin input
Run an unattended, reproducible JSON transformationjq and a shell script

Keep surrounding evidence

Text searches can match a word in any part of a line; structured filters target a named field when the format exposes it. If the error still does not explain the incident, use //error to retain the preceding line or open the selected result’s context with Ctrl+G. For request chains, inspect a correlation ID across two files instead of assuming adjacent lines belong together.

Check before replacing a pipeline

Flik is a local, interactive terminal application for macOS and Linux. It does not execute jq programs, manage central log retention or replace an unattended log-processing job. Keep automated transformations in the tools that already express them clearly, and use the interactive workspace when each result changes the next question.
